Theme

Money, work & business

luxury noun

also luxurious, luxuries, a luxury, live in luxury, in the lap of luxury, extravagance, lavish living

classical

Cic. Mur. 76: ōdit populus Rōmānus prīvātam luxuriam (Lewis & Short)
Sen. Ep. 18.4

luxuria, luxuriae f.

noun, first declension

luxury, extravagance

Lavish living and spending, usually with disapproval: Cicero sets private luxuria against public magnificentia. Its first sense is the rank growth of plants (Verg. G. 1.112).

Other words

  • luxus, luxūs m. — luxury, excess; splendour

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 4.7.42: adulēscēns luxū perditus (Lewis & Short); Verg. A. 1.637: rēgālī splendida luxū (Lewis & Short)

    Like luxuria, of excess in eating and drinking; in Virgil also, without blame, royal splendour.

  • lautitia, lautitiae f. — elegance, fine living

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 9.16.8: fāma ad tē dē meā novā lautitiā veniet (Lewis & Short)

    The elegance of a well-kept house and a good table, without the moral blame of luxuria; Cicero uses it of himself, joking.

  • dēliciae, dēliciārum f. pl. — luxuries, delights, comforts

    noun, first declension, plural · also used · classical · Cic. Mur. 13: multārum dēliciārum comes est extrēma saltātiō (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. enjoy: live it up (in dēliciīs vīvere)

    Things that delight the senses; in dēliciīs vīvere is “to live in luxury” (Vulg. Apoc. 18.9, cited by Morgan–Owens). The same word is also “darling” (dēliciae meae).

  • luxuriōsus, luxuriōsa, luxuriōsum — luxurious, given to luxury

    adjective, declension · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 2.66 (Lewis & Short)

    Of people and their way of life, extravagant; of crops, rank. For a luxurious thing, lautus (elegant, sumptuous) or sūmptuōsus (costly) is often the better word.

Examples

  • licet enim sine luxuriā agere fēstum diem

    for you can keep a holiday without extravaganceSen. Ep. 18.4

  • multa et lauta supellex, nōn illa quidem luxuriōsī hominis, sed tamen abundantis

    plenty of fine furniture, not that of a man of luxury, but of one who had more than enoughCic. Phil. 2.66 (Lewis & Short)

See also rich, resources, expensive.
